title: What the Talmud is
hook: the Mishnah, gathered around 200 CE, and centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side

segments.voice: Yesterday: the chasid, who says what's mine is yours, and our last saying from Pirkei Avot for now. Your line was what's mine is yours. Today, a new part of the path.

Picture a page unlike any other. In the middle, a small block of text. Wrapped around it, on the inside edge, a column in a different typeface. On the outside edge, another. Around those, smaller notes, cross-references, tiny letters in the margins. It looks like a city seen from the air: an old town in the center, neighborhoods growing out in every direction. That's a page of Talmud. For the next few weeks, i'll give you a taste of it. And the first surprise: you've already been reading part of it.
screen: `A PAGE UNLIKE ANY OTHER.` → `A CITY FROM THE AIR.` → `A TASTE OF TALMUD.`

segments.voice: Start with the old town in the center. Remember Rabbi Judah the Prince, who taught that small commandments count? Around the year two hundred, he gathered generations of oral teaching into one book, the Mishnah. It has six orders: farming and blessings, festivals, marriage and family, damages, holy things, and purity. Pirkei Avot, the sayings you just finished, is one small tractate of it. Then the rabbis kept talking. For the next few centuries, in the academies of the land of Israel and of Babylonia, they studied every line of the Mishnah and argued over it, in Hebrew and mostly in Aramaic. That discussion is the Gemara. Mishnah plus Gemara: the Talmud. There are two. The Jerusalem Talmud, from the land of Israel, and the larger Babylonian Talmud, the one most people mean. The word comes from the Hebrew root for learning and teaching. Here's what makes it unlike most holy books. It keeps the arguments. When two sages disagree, both opinions stay on the page, often with the losing side's reasons carefully preserved. Of the schools of Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says: these and these are the words of the living God. And the page keeps growing. When it was printed in Venice in the fifteen-twenties, the layout put Rashi's commentary on the inner edge and the Tosafot, later scholars from France and Germany, on the outer. Later editions added more. One page, voices from many centuries, all talking at once.
screen: `THE MISHNAH: AROUND 200 CE.` · `THE GEMARA: CENTURIES OF DEBATE.` · `BOTH OPINIONS STAY ON THE PAGE.` · `RASHI INSIDE, TOSAFOT OUTSIDE.` · then, large: `A CONVERSATION ACROSS CENTURIES.`

segments.voice: Imagine the small block at the center of the page: a question someone asked almost two thousand years ago. Around it, a sage answering, another disagreeing, and Rashi, a French commentator nearly nine hundred years later, writing in the margin. At the very edge there's room for you; what question would you add?
Talmud. Learning: the Mishnah and the centuries of discussion around it, printed with commentaries on every side.
Your line: a conversation across centuries. Both sides stay on the page. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Jews study Talmud in pairs (chavruta), reading aloud and arguing through each passage, in yeshivas, synagogues, and study groups; some learn one page every day.

notes: Review pass: the review line said yesterday (Avot 5:10) was 'the end of Pirkei Avot'; Avot continues past 5:10 (and has a sixth chapter), so it now says 'our last saying from Pirkei Avot for now'.
'Around the year 200' for the Mishnah; the Jerusalem Talmud c. 400 and the Babylonian c. 500–600 are conventional dates, left out of the voice except for the Mishnah.
Six orders glossed as farming and blessings (Zeraim, which opens with Berakhot), festivals (Moed), marriage and family (Nashim), damages (Nezikin), holy things (Kodashim), purity (Tohorot); confirm.
'These and these are the words of the living God': Eruvin 13b; paraphrased (not in quotation marks).
Daniel Bomberg's Venice edition (1520–23) fixed the pagination and the Rashi/Tosafot layout; confirm. Later editions (notably Vilna, Romm, 1880s) added more commentaries.
Pirkei Avot has no Gemara in the Babylonian Talmud; not stated in the script.
Audit (second sample): the practice put Rashi 'a thousand years' after the Mishnah (about 200 CE to about 1075); now 'nearly nine hundred years later'.
